Regarding the following two lines that clarify how the teaching of ultimate truth does not contradict worldly truth: the first line explains that the teaching of ultimate truth does not contradict the existence of results, while the latter line explains that the teaching of ultimate truth does not contradict the existence of causes.
The statement, "In teaching the Dharma, it is neither existent nor non-existent," refers to the ability to expound the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
This clarifies that the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) constitutes the ultimate truth.

Ultimate truth is free from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and likewise free from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); it is called "not existent" because it is existent while being devoid of a real intrinsic nature. Therefore, it is said to be "not non-existent," as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.

Furthermore, from the perspective of relative truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), things are said to exist or not exist based on their mutual dependence; however, when one reaches the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), all oppositions vanish, and they can no longer be termed existent or non-existent.
To say that "all phenomena arise by way of causes and conditions" does not contradict conventional truth.

From the perspective of ultimate truth, although it is said that things are neither existent nor non-existent, in accordance with worldly convention, it is constantly taught that results are obtained from causes; therefore, it is said that "all phenomena arise through conditions.
This means that by virtue of their wholesome or unwholesome causes and conditions, the phenomena of suffering and happiness arise.
The phrase "no self, no agent, and no recipient" refers to that which can explain the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
This clarifies that the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) constitutes the ultimate truth.
Within this reality, no self or person can be apprehended; thus, it is called "selflessness" (*anātman*).
Because there is no self, there is no person who acts as a cause; this is called "no creator.
Because there is no person who receives the fruit, it is called "no recipient.

As for the statement, "the karma of good and evil does not perish": although it does not exist within ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it constantly functions within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) to draw forth its results; therefore, it is said not to perish.
From here below is the second section, which praises his power of transformation.
First, there is a specific praise, followed by a general conclusion of reverence: "I constantly pay homage to the ocean of Dharma.
Within the preceding part, there is first a praise of the beginning of his transformation.
"By means of this wondrous Dharma, he delivers all living beings. This concludes the praise for his transformative work.
Furthermore, the preceding section praised the transformation through the teachings of the Hīnayāna, while the subsequent section praises his transformation through the teachings of the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, within the preceding section, there is first a specific eulogy;
the passage beginning with "The Three Jewels" concludes it collectively.
Within the specific portion, the appearance of the Buddha Jewel in the world is elucidated.
Regarding the phrase "At first, beneath the Bodhi tree, he subdued Māra by his power," this refers to the skillful means for attaining Buddhahood.

The Buddha attained enlightenment in reliance upon a tree; that tree upon which he relied is sometimes called the *buddha-vṛkṣa* (Buddha-tree), sometimes the *bodhi-vṛkṣa* (Way-tree), and at other times the *bodhi-vṛkṣa* (Enlightenment-tree).

Attaining Buddhahood beneath a tree is called the Buddha-tree; attaining the Way beneath a tree is referred to as the Way-tree; and realizing the fruit of Bodhi beneath a tree is named the Bodhi-tree.
Because he entrusted his final accomplishment to this [place], it is said that "it began here.

At that time, fearing that the Buddha’s Way would be perfected, Māra came to disturb and confuse the Bodhisattva; the Bodhisattva then entered the Samādhi of Supreme Benevolent Intent and, through his supernatural power, subdued Māra—an event known as "Subduing Māra by Power."
Furthermore, because the power of loving-kindness causes Māra to be subdued, it is called "Subduing Māra by Power.
Regarding the phrase "attaining the extinction of ambrosia and accomplishing the path of awakening," this precisely clarifies the attainment of Buddhahood.
To attain the extinction of ambrosia (*amṛta-nirodha*) is to clearly realize the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
Just as worldly ambrosia can remove parching thirst, the nirvana of the truth of cessation can eliminate craving; therefore, it is metaphorically named the "extinction of ambrosia."
Because one realizes through transformation according to conditions, it is called "attainment.
The phrase "the path of awakening is accomplished" clarifies the attainment of the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
"Awakening" refers to the Buddha, and "path" refers to Bodhi; this signifies that [enlightenment] has been definitively achieved and perfected.
The preceding attainment of this accomplishment refers to the left and right [ears].
